content: Cervical incompetence is a medical condition in which a pregnant woman’s cervix begins to dilate (widen) and efface (thin) prematurely, before the pregnancy has reached full term. This condition is a significant cause of miscarriage and preterm birth, particularly during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy. In cases of cervical incompetence, the dilation and effacement of the cervix occur without the presence of pain or uterine contractions. Unlike the normal physiological process of labor, where these changes are triggered by uterine contractions, cervical incompetence arises due to a structural weakness in the cervix. This weakness causes the cervix to open under the increasing pressure exerted by the growing uterus as the pregnancy progresses. If these changes are not addressed, they can lead to the rupture of the membranes and the delivery of a premature infant. According to data from the Mayo Clinic, cervical incompetence is relatively uncommon in the United States, affecting only 1–2% of all pregnancies. However, it is estimated to account for as many as 20–25% of miscarriages that occur during the second trimester. Risk Factors Several risk factors are associated with an increased likelihood of preterm birth or stillbirth due to cervical incompetence. These include: A prior diagnosis of cervical incompetence in a previous pregnancy. A history of preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM). A history of cervical conization (a surgical procedure involving the removal of a cone-shaped section of the cervix, often for biopsy purposes). Exposure to diethylstilbestrol (DES), a synthetic estrogen that can cause anatomical defects in the reproductive tract. Uterine anomalies or structural abnormalities. Additionally, repeated cervical procedures, such as mechanical dilation (especially during late pregnancy), may increase the risk of cervical incompetence. Any significant trauma to the cervix can also weaken the cervical tissues, further predisposing a woman to this condition. Treatment Cervical incompetence is typically treated only when it poses a threat to the pregnancy. One of the primary treatment options is cervical cerclage, a surgical procedure designed to reinforce the cervix. This is achieved by placing sutures around the cervix, above its opening, to narrow the cervical canal and provide additional support. The most common approach to cerclage involves accessing the cervix through the vagina using a speculum. Alternatively, a transabdominal cerclage can be performed, which involves placing the sutures through an abdominal incision. This method allows for precise placement of the stitch at the required level, making it particularly useful in cases where the cervix is very short, effaced, or severely distorted. Complications associated with cerclage are rare but have been documented in the medical literature. These include hemorrhage resulting from damage to veins during the procedure and fetal death due to occlusion of uterine vessels.
